subtitle: National Legislation and Judicial Systems · Human Rights and the Elimination of Forced Labor

blocks.narration: Welcome to the complete video guide to the History of Uzbekistan, weeks five and six. Two great themes lie ahead: how an independent state wrote its Constitution and built its courts, and how it confronted, and then dismantled, forced and child labor. By the end, you will know the dates, the numbers, and the ideas that examiners love, from the Avesta to the Constitution of nineteen ninety-two, and from the ILO conventions to the cotton fields. Let us begin.

blocks.title: The Road to the 1992 Constitution
blocks.subtitle: From the Declaration of Independence to the Basic Law
blocks.narration: Chapter one. Where does a state's freedom actually get written down? For Uzbekistan, the answer is a single document adopted in December nineteen ninety-two. This chapter follows the whole road to the Constitution: the commission, the drafts, the nationwide discussion, and the eleventh session that finally said yes.

blocks.heading: The Constitutional Commission
bullets: A commission of 64 under I. A. Karimov
blocks.narration: How do you write a constitution from scratch? The idea was born with the Declaration of Independence of June twentieth, nineteen ninety: the session of the Supreme Council that adopted it created a commission of sixty-four people headed by the first President, Islam Karimov. On July second and third, nineteen ninety-two, the composition was renewed to seventy-one members. The meeting of April twelfth, nineteen ninety-one, launched the direct work: a working group of thirty-two people and six small groups with fifty researchers, divided by theme. Constitutions of the USA, Germany, France, Turkey, Japan, Lithuania, and drafts of seven CIS republics, were studied; of three concepts, the President's rule-of-law concept became the basis.

blocks.heading: From 158 Articles to 127
blocks.narration: How long should a constitution be? The first answer: one hundred fifty-eight articles in six sections, ready by October and November of nineteen ninety-one. The decisive impulse was the constitutional law 'On the Foundations of State Independence' of August thirty-first, nineteen ninety-one, seventeen articles. In spring nineteen ninety-two came a second version of one hundred forty-nine articles, then a third of one hundred thirty-seven. For the nationwide discussion, a text of one hundred twenty-seven articles was published. The draft was first compiled in Russian, then translated into Uzbek in July and August of nineteen ninety-two. Every version was read and corrected by hand by the chairman; as Academician Orazayev recalled, the President read the draft again and again.

blocks.heading: The Draft Becomes a Constitution
blocks.narration: Let us put the whole journey on one line. June twentieth, nineteen ninety: the Declaration of Independence, and the decision to write a constitution. August thirty-first, nineteen ninety-one: the constitutional law on the foundations of state independence, seventeen articles. October to November nineteen ninety-one: the first draft, one hundred fifty-eight articles. September twenty-sixth, nineteen ninety-two: the draft is published for the nation. November twenty-first, nineteen ninety-two: a second publication, a precedent of two-stage discussion. And finally, December eighth, nineteen ninety-two: the eleventh session of the Supreme Council adopts the Constitution. Each step narrowed the text and widened the circle of people involved.

blocks.heading: The Two-Stage Nationwide Discussion
blocks.narration: Who gets to shape a constitution? In Uzbekistan, everyone. From late September to early December nineteen ninety-two, the draft was debated in newspapers, on radio and television, in collectives and student classrooms. Letters came from scientists and pensioners, workers and dehkans, military and religious figures. More than six thousand proposals arrived; the commission alone received more than a thousand letters. The result: corrections to sixty of the one hundred twenty-seven articles, four articles excluded, several new ones added. On November twenty-first the draft was published a second time, a precedent of two-stage nationwide discussion.

blocks.heading: What Changed at the Eleventh Session
blocks.narration: Adoption day was no formality. On December eighth, nineteen ninety-two, the deputies made about eighty changes and clarifications. The terms of the Constitutional, Supreme and Higher Economic Courts were cut from ten years to five. Article sixty-four, today sixty-five, gained the words that motherhood and childhood are under the protection of the state, proposed by deputy Khalimakhon Usmanova. Article twenty-six fixed the presumption of innocence, article twenty-seven the secrecy of correspondence. The Arbitration Court became the Economic Court, and the parliament was named the Oliy Majlis. The commission, meanwhile, rejected bicameralism and mandatory union membership.

blocks.heading: Why a People's Law
blocks.problem: Why does the author call the 1992 Constitution a truly people's law?

steps.text: Sept 26, 1992: the draft is published for all
Debate in press, radio, TV, workplaces

blocks.result: A Basic Law debated by the whole nation
blocks.narration: A typical exam question: prove that the Constitution was a people's law. Step one: on September twenty-sixth, nineteen ninety-two, the draft was published in the press, open to everyone. Step two: the debate ran in newspapers, on radio and television, in collectives and student auditoriums. Step three: more than six thousand proposals arrived, and more than a thousand letters to the commission alone. Step four: the response was real, corrections to sixty of one hundred twenty-seven articles, four articles removed. Step five: on November twenty-first the draft was published a second time, a precedent of two-stage discussion. A law debated letter by letter by the whole nation, that is what people's law means.

Chapter one in four lines. The Declaration of June twentieth, nineteen ninety, created a commission of sixty-four under Karimov. The draft shrank from one hundred fifty-eight to one hundred twenty-seven articles. On December eighth, nineteen ninety-two, the eleventh session of the Supreme Council adopted the Constitution, with about eighty amendments made right at the session. A people's law, born of a two-stage national discussion.

chapters.title: Justice from the Avesta to the Khanates

blocks.title: Justice from the Avesta to the Khanates
blocks.subtitle: Courts before the Russian conquest
blocks.narration: Chapter two. How deep do the roots of Uzbek justice go? Deeper than most people imagine. Before empires and ideologies, the Avesta already knew what a court was for. This chapter walks through ancient law, Muslim law, and the judicial world of the Bukhara and Khiva khanates.

blocks.heading: The Avesta: Justice Before the Khanates
bullets: An ancient cultural and legal source
The court checked the claim's validity
blocks.narration: Where does the story of Uzbek courts begin? In a text most people know as scripture. The Avesta, one of the ancient cultural and legal sources of the region, already contained rules concerning judicial cases. Three tasks stand out, and they are on the screen: the court determined the guilt of the perpetrator, the validity of the claim, and the punishment. Guilt, claim, punishment, the same three questions every modern court still asks. So the story of Uzbek justice starts not with statutes, but with the Avesta. That is the starting point.

blocks.heading: The Early States and Their Laws
bullets: Each state kept its own legal system
blocks.narration: Which states held this land before the khanates? The Saka, the Kangju, the Huns, the Sarmatians, then the Karluk Khaganate and the Turkic Khaganate. Each of them had its own legal system, its own rules, courts and punishments. But the article makes an honest note: these systems often rested on prejudices rather than on evidence. Law existed, yet it was interwoven with belief and with custom. Keep that baseline in mind, for it is the yardstick against which every later system, Muslim, imperial and Soviet, should be measured. That is where the next chapter begins.

blocks.heading: Muslim Law: One Judge, All Cases
blocks.narration: What changed with Muslim law? Classification, first: crimes were now classified from religious and ideological positions, so the question of what kind of act this was got its answer through faith. And structure, second: a single judge handled all criminal and family-inheritance cases. No division into criminal chambers and family chambers, one figure, one bench, full jurisdiction. Contrast this with the specialized systems of the empire and the Soviets: from one judge for everything, to a whole architecture of courts. One judge, all cases: a simple formula, and a telling one.

blocks.heading: Judicial Power in the Khanates
blocks.narration: Now the khanates, Bukhara and Khiva. At the top of judicial power stood the emirs and khans themselves. They conducted public proceedings, mainly concerning non-payment of taxes, plunder of the treasury, and rebellions. Around them stood a pyramid of judges, exactly as the table shows: the kushbegi, the beks, the qazi-kalon, the supreme judge, and the qazi-askar, the military judge. The formula is precise: they held all rights except the right of life and death. That right belonged to one person only. Only the khan could pass a death sentence, and for the death penalty his permission was required.

blocks.heading: Who Could Pass a Death Sentence?
blocks.problem: In the Bukhara and Khiva khanates, who had the right to pass a death sentence?

steps.text: Emirs and khans headed judicial power
Their rights stopped at life and death
Only the khan (emir) passed death sentences

blocks.narration: A classic test question, so answer it like a lawyer. Who could pass a death sentence in the khanates? Step one: recall who ran justice. The emirs and khans stood at the head of judicial power and held the public proceedings. Step two: recall the judges beneath them, the kushbegi, the beks, the qazi-kalon and the qazi-askar. Step three: recall the limit, their powers covered everything except the right of life and death. Step four: draw the conclusion. For the death penalty the permission of the khan, the emir, was required, which means only the khan could pass a death sentence. Say it exactly that way in the exam, word for word.

items: Early states: own laws, prejudices too
Muslim law: one judge, all cases
blocks.narration: Chapter two in brief. The court of the Avesta decided guilt, the validity of the claim, and the punishment. The early states, from the Saka to the Turkic Khaganate, kept their own legal systems, often based on prejudices. Under Muslim law, a single judge handled all criminal and family-inheritance cases. And in the khanates, only the khan could pass a death sentence; every other judge stopped at the right of life and death.

chapters.title: Courts under the Empire and the Soviets

blocks.title: Courts under the Empire and the Soviets
blocks.subtitle: Turkestan 1865–1917, then 1917–1960
blocks.narration: Chapter three. What happens to a legal system when the state itself changes hands? Twice in half a century, the courts of this land were rebuilt from above, first by the Russian Empire, then by the Soviets. Two empires, two logics, one territory.

blocks.heading: Imperial Justice in Turkestan
blocks.narration: Follow the empire's steps. Eighteen sixty-five: the Temporary Provision defines the procedure for introducing Russian justice. Eighteen sixty-seven: the Draft Provision on the Organization of the Judicial Branch, in three parts, introduces a two-tier imperial system. June twelfth, eighteen eighty-six: the emperor approves the Provision on the Administration of the Turkestan Region, from now on the main legal document of the region. Eighteen ninety-seven to ninety-nine: the reforms create a judicial chamber, the highest instance, with control functions. And from eighteen ninety-eight to nineteen seventeen, the fourth stage adapts the system to the Judicial Statutes of the empire. The empire wrote the rules, and the region adapted.

blocks.heading: Two Court Systems Side by Side
bullets: Qazi and biy courts for nomads
blocks.narration: Was colonial justice uniform? Not at all; it ran on parallel tracks. General courts, built on the laws of the empire, operated alongside courts based on sharia. For the nomadic population, the old courts of the qazis and the biys were preserved. And some figures combined roles we would separate today: the district judge considered minor cases and at the same time conducted the preliminary investigation. The reforms of eighteen ninety-seven to ninety-nine added a judicial chamber, the highest instance of the region, while conciliatory judges, district, additional and honorary, could order arrest for up to three days.

blocks.heading: 1917: The Old Courts Are Suspended
blocks.narration: Then comes the revolution. The decree of December nineteen seventeen suspended the district courts, the Tashkent judicial chamber, and the military courts, the whole imperial structure. What replaced them? People's courts, tribunals and revolutionary tribunals appeared, and their purpose was open: punishing those unsympathetic to Bolshevik ideology. Yet even this radical government had to compromise. Under pressure from public protests, the Soviets preserved the courts of the qazis and biys, and in nineteen twenty-two adopted the Provision on the Court of Qadis of the Turkestan Republic. The old law died slowly.

blocks.heading: The Soviet Codes, 1922–1960
blocks.narration: Now watch Soviet procedure being built, code by code. On August first, nineteen twenty-two, the first systematic Code of Criminal Procedure came into force. The code of nineteen twenty-six established judicial control over detention and the dismissal of cases, in articles two hundred one, two hundred two and two hundred forty-four. The code of nineteen twenty-nine simplified the procedure, but allowed the court itself to draw up the indictment. Finally, on the basis of the Fundamentals of Criminal Justice of nineteen fifty-eight, a new code was approved on May twenty-first, nineteen fifty-nine, and entered practice on January first, nineteen sixty.

blocks.heading: From Decree to Code
blocks.problem: How did criminal procedure in Uzbekistan develop between 1917 and 1960?

steps.text: May 21, 1959: new CPC, in force Jan 1, 1960

blocks.narration: Examiners love this arc, so rehearse it as a chain, from nineteen seventeen to nineteen sixty. December nineteen seventeen: the decree suspends the imperial courts; people's courts and tribunals take over. August first, nineteen twenty-two: the first systematic Code of Criminal Procedure enters force. Nineteen twenty-six: judicial control over detention is fixed in articles two hundred one, two hundred two and two hundred forty-four. Nineteen twenty-nine: the process is simplified, but the court may draw up the indictment itself. May twenty-first, nineteen fifty-nine: a new code is approved, and from January first, nineteen sixty, it governs practice. Decree, code, control, simplification, new code: memorize the chain. Five links, five dates, one story.

items: 1886: Region law, the main legal document
General, sharia, qazi and biy courts
New CPC in force from Jan 1, 1960
blocks.narration: Chapter three in four lines. The Provision approved on June twelfth, eighteen eighty-six, became the region's main legal document. General courts, sharia courts, and the qazi and biy courts of the nomads worked side by side. In December nineteen seventeen, the imperial courts were suspended and people's courts appeared. And the new Code of Criminal Procedure, approved in nineteen fifty-nine, has governed practice since January first, nineteen sixty.

chapters.title: The 1938 Law and the War Years

blocks.title: The 1938 Law and the War Years
blocks.subtitle: The Uzbek SSR judiciary, 1937–1945
blocks.narration: Chapter four. Two shocks hit the courts of the Uzbek SSR within a single decade: the law of nineteen thirty-eight, which rebuilt the whole judicial system, and the war of nineteen forty-one to forty-five, which tested it to breaking point. Here, numbers tell the story better than adjectives.

blocks.heading: The Law of August 16, 1938
bullets: Adopted by the Supreme Soviet of the USSR
blocks.narration: On August sixteenth, nineteen thirty-eight, the second session of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR adopted the law 'On the Judicial System of the USSR, Union and Autonomous Republics': eight chapters, eighty articles, built on the Constitution of nineteen thirty-six. The law split the courts in two. The all-Union courts: the Supreme Court of the USSR, military tribunals, railway and water transport courts. The courts of the Union republics: people's, regional and Supreme Courts. People's judges were elected by district citizens for three years, from the age of twenty-three, while regional and Supreme Courts were elected for five. The Plenum of the Supreme Court met at least once every two months.

blocks.heading: The Uzbek SSR's Courts in Late 1939
blocks.narration: Now map that law onto the republic. In the second half of nineteen thirty-nine, the Uzbek SSR had two hundred twenty-six people's courts; only one was closed, for lack of specialists. Two hundred twenty-five people's judges served; just seventeen of them had higher education, and forty-six were women. Above them stood five regional courts, in Tashkent, Samarkand, Fergana, Khorezm and Bukhara, plus the Surkhandarya District Court with sixty-eight judges. Read the table as a diagnosis: the network was wide, but the profession was thin. And that thin profession was about to face a war.

blocks.heading: Weak Cadres
blocks.narration: How bad was the staffing crisis? Numbers again. In nineteen thirty-seven to thirty-nine, five hundred forty-one judges were dismissed. Of all people's judges, only six served their full term, two point six percent. The People's Commissar of Justice, Turdiev, recorded cases of judges colluding with criminals. People's courts sat in unsuitable buildings, mosques and warehouses. And for the judge Inoyatov, half of the decisions and most of the verdicts were overturned on appeal. When you hear about the war years next, remember this starting point: the system entered the war already exhausted.

blocks.heading: Military Tribunals at War
blocks.narration: On June twenty-second, nineteen forty-one, the very day of Germany's invasion, two regulations were adopted: 'On the State of War' and 'On Military Tribunals.' Their rules were brutal in their simplicity. The trial had to begin within twenty-four hours after the accused was brought to trial. The death sentence was announced after seventy-two hours. Cassation was prohibited; a verdict could change only in the supervisory procedure. Until nineteen forty-three, tribunals had three permanent members without people's assessors, appointed, not elected. Cases were heard mostly behind closed doors. Yet execution could be postponed until the end of combat operations: the convicted washed away their guilt with blood at the front.

blocks.heading: The Judiciary During the War
blocks.narration: The war squeezed the courts from both sides. July fifteenth, nineteen forty-one: a decree cuts staffing; judges' leaves are canceled, and people's courts are reduced by twenty percent in rural areas and twenty-five percent in cities. In nineteen forty-two, twenty-eight people's courts were closed; mobilization took twenty to thirty percent of judges in some regions, in Fergana eight of twenty-four. The system adapted: the Tashkent Law Institute resumed in nineteen forty-two, and in August nineteen forty-three four-month courses opened in Tashkent, six-month courses in Samarkand. In September nineteen forty-four, a Congress of Judges discussed theft and the cotton harvest. By the end of nineteen forty-five, only fifty-six lawyers with higher education remained in the people's courts.

blocks.heading: How the War Reshaped the Courts
blocks.problem: How did June 22, 1941 change the judicial system of the Uzbek SSR?

steps.text: By late 1945: only 56 lawyers with degrees

blocks.narration: Let us turn the war years into a cause-and-effect chain. The cause: June twenty-second, nineteen forty-one, Germany invades, and the two war regulations are adopted the same day. The immediate effects: trials within twenty-four hours, death sentences announced after seventy-two, cassation prohibited. The administrative effects: the decree of July fifteenth cuts staff and courts, twenty percent in the countryside, twenty-five percent in cities, twenty-eight courts gone by nineteen forty-two. The response: education, the Law Institute reopens, courses start in Tashkent and Samarkand. The outcome: by the end of nineteen forty-five, only fifty-six lawyers with higher education remain in the people's courts. War made justice faster, harsher, and thinner. Remember the numbers.

Chapter four, compressed. The law of August sixteenth, nineteen thirty-eight: eight chapters, eighty articles. In nineteen thirty-nine: two hundred twenty-six people's courts, but only seventeen of two hundred twenty-five judges with higher education. Tribunals: trial in twenty-four hours, death sentence after seventy-two, no cassation. And by the end of the war, just fifty-six lawyers with degrees remained in the people's courts.

chapters.title: Four Stages of the Legal System

blocks.title: Four Stages of the Legal System
blocks.subtitle: Independent Uzbekistan from 1991
blocks.narration: Chapter five. Independent Uzbekistan did not build its legal system in one leap; scholars count four distinct stages. What changed in each one, and why does the fourth stage begin in twenty seventeen? Keep the dates in mind, they are pure exam material.

blocks.heading: Four Stages at a Glance
blocks.narration: Here is Azizov's whole classification on one screen. Stage one, nineteen ninety-one to two thousand: the transitional period, forming the foundations of national statehood. Stage two, two thousand one to two thousand nine: democratic renewal. Stage three, twenty ten to twenty sixteen: deepening democratic reforms, about fifty laws. Stage four, from twenty seventeen: the Strategy of Actions. Four stages, four ambitions. Notice the rhythm, roughly a decade each, and each one answering the unfinished business of the one before it. The dates themselves are a favorite test question. Learn them as a rhythm, not as a list.

blocks.heading: Stage One: Building the Foundations
blocks.narration: Stage one, nineteen ninety-one to two thousand: the transitional period. Its legal pillars: the constitutional law 'On the Foundations of State Independence' of August thirty-first, nineteen ninety-one, seventeen articles, the legal foundation of independence; then the Constitution of nineteen ninety-two; and then entirely new branches of law. Between nineteen ninety-four and two thousand eight, fifteen codes were adopted. Think of the scale: a state that had inherited Soviet law rewrote its own foundations, constitution first, codes after. That is what building statehood means in legal terms. Fifteen codes in fourteen years: remember the number.

blocks.heading: Stage Two: Democratic Renewal
blocks.narration: Stage two, two thousand one to two thousand nine: democratic renewal. The parliament became bicameral. In two thousand seven, two changes came together: the death penalty was abolished, and the sanction for arrest was transferred to the courts, no arrest without a judge. The humanizing effect was measurable. Seventy-five percent of serious crimes were reclassified as less serious, and by two thousand six the number of sentences was twenty percent lower than in the year two thousand. Reform, in other words, showed up in the cold statistics of the courts.

blocks.heading: Stages Three and Four
bullets: Supreme Council of Judges; one court
blocks.narration: Stage three, twenty ten to twenty sixteen: implementing the Concept of Deepening Democratic Reforms, about fifty laws. Stage four, from twenty seventeen: the Strategy of Actions, in which judicial and legal reform is the second national priority. Its results: a Supreme Council of Judges; the Supreme Court and the Higher Economic Court merged into one unified Supreme Court; seventy-one economic courts; judges appointed first for five years, then ten, then life. Torture is prohibited. President Mirziyoyev put it plainly: ensuring the genuine independence of the judiciary is our number one priority. Lex.uz now holds ninety-nine thousand seven hundred six documents.

blocks.heading: Citizens Join Lawmaking
blocks.narration: Who writes the laws in stage four? Increasingly, everyone. After the President's address of December twenty-third, twenty seventeen, the 'My Opinion' portal was launched, with four hundred forty collective appeals published. On the Ministry of Justice portal, about eight thousand acts were considered, including five hundred fifty-seven bills and two thousand three hundred eighty draft government resolutions, and thirty-five thousand proposals. Youth gained a voice: a Youth Parliament under the Legislative Chamber, formalized on June twenty-ninth, twenty twenty. And on February twenty-seventh, twenty twenty, a Parliamentary Commission was established to monitor the Sustainable Development Goals up to twenty thirty.

blocks.heading: What Changed After 2017
blocks.problem: Name the concrete judicial reforms of the fourth stage, from 2017.

steps.text: Two supreme courts merged into one

blocks.result: An independent judiciary as goal number one
blocks.narration: A favorite question: what exactly did the fourth stage change? Answer in five steps. One: a Supreme Council of Judges was created, so judges gained self-governance. Two: the Supreme Court and the Higher Economic Court merged into a single Supreme Court. Three: seventy-one economic courts now operate across the country. Four: the terms of office changed, first five years, then ten, then a life appointment. Five: torture was prohibited outright. And the frame around it all: within the Strategy of Actions, judicial and legal reform stands as the second priority, while, as President Mirziyoyev said, genuine independence of the judiciary is priority number one. That is the fourth stage, step by step.

Chapter five in four lines. Four stages begin in nineteen ninety-one, two thousand one, twenty ten and twenty seventeen. In two thousand seven the death penalty was abolished and arrest sanctions moved to the courts. Since twenty seventeen: a unified Supreme Court, a Supreme Council of Judges, and life appointments for judges. The system is still evolving, and that is exactly the point.

blocks.title: What Is Forced Labor?
blocks.subtitle: ILO Conventions No. 29 and No. 105
blocks.narration: Chapter six. From courts to rights. What exactly is forced labor, and when is work legal even if it is hard? The answers were written in Geneva, in Convention twenty-nine and Convention one hundred five of the International Labour Organization. Definitions first, judgments after.

blocks.heading: Convention No. 29 Defines Forced Labor
bullets: All work exacted under threat of penalty
From any person, adult or child
blocks.narration: Here is the definition every student must quote, from Convention twenty-nine, adopted in nineteen thirty. Forced or compulsory labor means all work or service which is exacted from any person under the threat of any penalty, and to which he has not offered himself voluntarily. Unpack it and you find four elements: work or service; any person, adult or child, citizen or migrant; involuntary nature; and threat of penalty, which need not be criminal, the loss of rights is enough. Article two also sets exceptions: military service, civic obligations, work under a court sentence, emergencies, and minor community works.

blocks.heading: Modern Slavery: the Numbers
bullets: Every fourth victim is a child
blocks.narration: Why does this matter globally? Look at the ILO estimates for twenty seventeen. Forty point three million people are in modern slavery. Of them, twenty-four point nine million are in forced labor, and fifteen point four million are in forced marriage. And the cruelest figure of all: every fourth victim is a child. Keep these three numbers firmly in mind. They are exactly the kind of figures that appear in multiple-choice questions, and they explain better than any speech why the conventions matter, and why the struggle continues. Now to the two conventions themselves.

blocks.heading: Convention No. 29 versus No. 105
blocks.narration: Two conventions, two different jobs. Convention twenty-nine, from nineteen thirty, defines forced labor and lists its exceptions; it bans forced labor in general. Convention one hundred five, from nineteen fifty-seven, goes further and demands its immediate abolition in five cases. As a means of political coercion or punishment for political opinions. As a method of mobilizing labor for economic development. As a means of labor discipline. As punishment for participation in strikes. And as a means of racial, social, national or religious discrimination. If the exam asks which convention bans forced labor as a tool of discipline, the answer is one hundred five.

blocks.heading: Uzbekistan's Ratifications
blocks.narration: As of January first, twenty twenty-one, Uzbekistan had ratified seventeen ILO conventions, eight of them fundamental, and one protocol: Convention twenty-nine and Convention one hundred five on forced labor, Convention one eighty-two on the worst forms of child labor, Convention one thirty-eight on minimum age, and the Protocol of twenty fourteen to Convention twenty-nine, ratified on June twenty-fifth, twenty nineteen, in force from September sixteenth, twenty twenty. The UN covenants of nineteen sixty-six were ratified too. But as Narbaeva stressed at the International Labour Conference, ratification is only fifty percent of the solution; the rest is implementation.

blocks.heading: The National Definition and Its Gap
bullets: Gap: the voluntary element is missing
blocks.narration: Now the national mirror. Article thirty-seven of the Constitution prohibits forced labor, except serving a sentence by court order and other cases provided by law. Article ten of the Labor Code allows ratified conventions to be applied directly. Article seven defines forced labor as performing work under the threat of any penalty, including as a means of maintaining labor discipline. But the authors spot a defect: the element of voluntary non-offering of services has been dropped, so coercion outside labor relations may escape the norm. Liability exists, under article fourteen eighty-two of the Criminal Code and article fifty-one of the Administrative Code, but only for administrative coercion.

blocks.heading: Hashar: Voluntary Work Only
bullets: Public works need a legal basis
blocks.narration: One Uzbek institution needs special care: hashar. The dictionary defines it as the voluntary, selfless participation of the majority in completing a task, neighbors gathering to build, to plant, to clean. Resolution three hundred forty-nine of the Cabinet of Ministers, of May tenth, twenty eighteen, allows involvement in public works, construction and agricultural included, only on a voluntary basis, and only with a document of the President or the Cabinet. The key factor is good will. Coercion to hashar under threat of punishment is a direct sign of forced labor; the authors propose to enshrine the definition of hashar in law.

blocks.heading: Applying the Four Elements
blocks.problem: Teachers are ordered to pick cotton, on pain of losing pay. Is this forced labor under Convention No. 29?

steps.text: Work or service? Yes: cotton picking
Voluntary? No: it is an order
Threat of penalty? Yes: losing pay

blocks.narration: Let us practice the definition. Teachers in a district are ordered to the cotton fields, and those who refuse risk losing pay. Forced labor or not? Run the four elements. Element one: work or service, yes, cotton picking is work. Element two: any person, yes, teachers are persons, and the convention covers everyone. Element three: involuntary nature, yes, this is an order, not a choice. Element four: threat of any penalty, yes, and the penalty need not be criminal, losing pay is enough. All four elements are present, so the conclusion follows: this is forced labor under Convention twenty-nine. Learn the method: check, check, check, check, conclude. Four checks, one verdict.

Chapter six in four lines. Forced labor has four elements: work, any person, involuntariness, and penalty. Convention one hundred five demands immediate abolition in five cases. Uzbekistan has ratified seventeen conventions plus one protocol. Article thirty-seven of the Constitution bans forced labor, and coerced hashar is forced labor, nothing less. Definitions first, judgments after; that is always the legal way.

blocks.title: Ending Forced and Child Labor
blocks.subtitle: Mechanisms, cotton, and results
blocks.narration: Chapter seven, the final chapter. Laws on paper, people in the fields. How did Uzbekistan actually dismantle forced and child labor, and what did the cotton monoculture have to do with it? This chapter connects the institutions, the monitoring, and the long history behind them.

blocks.heading: Three Types of Mechanisms
blocks.narration: Who fights forced labor today? Three types of mechanisms work in parallel. First, the collegial bodies: the National Commission on Combating Trafficking in Persons and Forced Labor, the Coordination Council on Child Labor, and the Republican Tripartite Commission on Social and Labor Issues. Second, the labor authorities: state labor inspections, created under the resolution of December thirty-first, twenty eighteen, and authorized to initiate cases and transfer materials to court. Third, civil society: trade unions and non-governmental organizations. Above them all, the Institute of the National Rapporteur reports annually to the President on forced labor.

blocks.heading: Building the Institutions
blocks.narration: The institutions grew in three periods. The first, nineteen ninety-two to two thousand seven: Uzbekistan joins the ILO, ratifies conventions twenty-nine and one hundred five, adopts the Labor Code and the Employment Law, creates labor inspections. The second, two thousand eight to twenty sixteen: international criticism produces the anti-trafficking law, resolutions two hundred seven, eighty-two and one hundred thirty-two, a Rehabilitation Center, and the Coordinating Council on Child Labor in twenty thirteen. The third, from twenty seventeen: criminal liability, a Parliamentary Commission from the Senate, and the National Commission with the National Rapporteur under the decree of July thirtieth, twenty nineteen. In twenty nineteen, two hundred fifty-nine cases were identified, fined seven hundred seventy-two million sums; for the twenty twenty campaign, forty-two officials were held accountable.

blocks.heading: The Monitoring Verdict
bullets: 2019: the issue is off the agenda
blocks.narration: Did all this work? Since twenty thirteen, child and forced labor in cotton has been monitored with ILO experts, the third-party monitoring project. The conclusion for twenty thirteen: child labor in cotton harvesting was not used systematically, although cases of forced labor were recognized. Independent monitoring for twenty fourteen to twenty eighteen went further: the systematic use of child labor has been eliminated. In twenty nineteen, the issue, as the report put it, was no longer on the agenda. That year, national monitoring ran for the first time with American and European trade unions, under the International Trade Union Confederation. From denial to verification: that is the arc.

blocks.heading: Cotton Monoculture's Long Roots
blocks.narration: Why was there so much cotton, and so much labor to extract? Bhat's article goes back to the empire. By nineteen eleven and twelve, Turkestan already supplied fifty-two percent of the needs of the Russian textile industry; by nineteen fourteen and fifteen, seventy percent. Between eighteen eighty-six and nineteen hundred, plantations grew from forty-one thousand to ninety-two thousand eight hundred eighty-eight dessiatines, and the railway that reached Tashkent in eighteen ninety-eight opened Central Asia to Russian capital. Uzbekistan later became the second largest producer and exporter, over eight hundred thousand tons annually, about sixty percent of Central Asia's cotton. The ecological price: irrigating one million four hundred seventy thousand hectares almost destroyed the Aral Sea, which kept fifteen percent of its volume and lost twenty-four species of endemic fish.

blocks.heading: Child Labor in the Cotton Fields
blocks.narration: Now the human cost, in numbers. According to the EJF, about two hundred thousand children worked annually in the Fergana Valley alone; UNICEF, in two thousand, found twenty-two point six percent of children aged five to fourteen in at least part-time work. During the harvest, schools closed for two to three months; children went to the fields from age seven, first the teenagers, then the twelve to fourteen-year-olds, and by late September even first-graders. The workday ran ten to twelve hours in heat up to forty-five degrees. Children drank from irrigation canals and lived in barracks without windows or doors. Pay fell from five dollars for five days to fifteen cents. In the Samarkand region, eight children died over two years.

blocks.heading: Causes, Losses, and the Response
blocks.narration: Why did this happen? The ILRF study of two thousand eight gives the uncomfortable answer: the roots lie not in poverty or tradition, but in the nature of the state and its control over rural society. A command economy with quotas pushes output above what the market would choose; without market incentives, coercion becomes necessary. Demechanization made it worse: machine harvesting fell from two-thirds to ten percent. Education paid the bill: over twenty percent of instructional time lost, and across grades five to nine, a full academic year. The response: cotton picking entered the list of worst forms of child labor in two thousand one; conventions one eighty-two and one thirty-eight were ratified in two thousand eight and two thousand nine; the two thousand seven law allows work from sixteen, from fifteen with parental consent, from fourteen light work outside school.

blocks.heading: Why Child Labor Became Systemic
blocks.problem: Why did child labor become mass-scale in the cotton sector?

steps.text: State quotas set output above market

blocks.narration: The last walkthrough, and the deepest question: why did child labor become mass-scale? Step one: the state set cotton quotas, pushing production above what the market would choose. Step two: without market incentives, someone must be compelled to work; coercion becomes a tool of policy. Step three: demechanization, with machine harvesting collapsing from two-thirds to ten percent, multiplied the demand for cheap hands. Step four: the khokimiyats organized the mobilization of children through the schools, quotas passed down to the individual child. Conclusion: systemic child labor was not a survival of tradition; it was produced by a command economy. Without agrarian reform, Bhat concludes, the problem cannot be solved. Remember the chain.

Chapter seven in four lines. Three periods of institution-building begin in nineteen ninety-two, two thousand eight and twenty seventeen. In twenty nineteen, two hundred fifty-nine cases of forced labor were identified, with seven hundred seventy-two million sums in fines. The ILO confirmed that systematic child labor has been eliminated. And the deep cause was economic: machine picking fell to ten percent, so hands were demanded instead.

Before we part, the whole of weeks five and six on one screen. The Constitution was adopted on December eighth, nineteen ninety-two, by the eleventh session of the Supreme Council. The courts traveled from the Avesta through the khanates, the empire, and the Soviet system. The law of nineteen thirty-eight counted eight chapters and eighty articles. Independent development ran through four stages. Forced labor is defined by four elements and banned in five cases. And systematic child labor in cotton was eliminated by twenty nineteen. You now hold the whole map.

blocks.message: You have covered all of weeks five and six — constitutions, courts, and the end of forced labor. Take the test — you are ready.
blocks.narration: That concludes the complete guide to weeks five and six of the History of Uzbekistan. You have walked the road from the Avesta to the Constitution, from military tribunals to labor inspectorates, and from the cotton fields to the ILO's verdict. Review the dates, trust the method, and take the test. Good luck. You are ready.
